claim: nhl-2 mRNA is highly expressed in the C. elegans germline
source: nhl-2 mRNA is reported to be highly expressed in the C. elegans germline (Ortiz et al., 2014; Reinke et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Ortiz et al., 2014; Reinke et al., 2004)

claim: nhl-2(ok818) displayed a significantly reduced brood size at 20°C, 23°C and 25°C compared to wild-type worms
source: At all three temperatures, compared to wild-type worms, nhl-2(ok818) displayed a significantly reduced brood size
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text

claim: nhl-2(ok818) showed a significant increase in embryonic lethality at 23°C and 25°C
source: at 23°C and 25°C there was a significant increase in embryonic lethality (Figure 1A,B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: nhl-2(ma372 ma399) mutants show comparable fertility defects to nhl-2(ok818)
source: Comparable results were obtained when we used a second nhl-2 null allele (nhl-2(ma372 ma399)) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B

claim: Temperature-dependent fertility defects have been described for several strong loss of function or null alleles of germline genes, including factors involved in small RNA pathways
source: This temperature-dependent fertility defect has been described for several strong loss of function or null alleles of germline genes, including factors involved in small RNA pathways (Phillips et al., 2012; Gu et al., 2009; van Wolfswinkel et al., 2009; Wang and Reinke, 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies

claim: nhl-2(ok818) mutants display abnormal chromosome morphology in diakinetic oocytes
source: nhl-2(ok818) worms possessed a range of chromosomal abnormalities including aggregation into disorganized clumps, and greater than six DAPI bodies (Figure 1C,D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D

claim: Wild-type diakinetic oocytes display six discrete DAPI bodies, indicative of homologous chromosome pairs
source: While wild-type diakinetic oocytes displayed six discrete DAPI bodies, indicative of homologous chromosome pairs
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about C. elegans chromosome organization and is supported by experimental observations

claim: nhl-2(ma372 ma399) mutants show similar diakinetic oocyte defects to nhl-2(ok818)
source: Similar results were obtained when we examined diakinetic oocyte of nhl-2(ma372 ma399) mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C

claim: NHL-2 is required for normal reproductive capacity and germline chromosome organization
source: Together these data indicate that NHL-2 is required for normal reproductive capacity and germline chromosome organization.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing reduced brood size and chromosome defects in nhl-2 mutants

claim: NHL-2 co-localizes with CGH-1 in perinuclear germ granules (P granules) and in the cytoplasmic core of the syncytial germline
source: We found that NHL-2 co-localizes with CGH-1 in the gonad in both perinuclear germ granules, known as P granules in C. elegans, and in the cytoplasmic core of the syncytial germline (Figure 1E- Figure 1—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A

claim: P granules are cytoplasmic aggregations of mRNA and protein that contribute to germ cell fate
source: P granules are cytoplasmic aggregations of mRNA and protein that contribute to germ cell fate, and many RNA regulatory pathways, including those involved in small RNA pathways, localize to these structures (Voronina et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work (Voronina et al., 2011)

claim: NHL-2 localizes to P granules in early-stage embryos and is quickly lost from the somatic lineages after the 4 cell stage
source: We also observed that NHL-2 localizes to P granules in early-stage embryos and was quickly lost from the somatic lineages after the 4 cell stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and data not shown)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B

claim: NHL-2 localization to P granules in early embryos is consistent with a previous study
source: consistent with a previous study (Hyenne et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work (Hyenne et al., 2008)

claim: The absence of NHL-2 does not affect P granule formation
source: First, the absence of NHL-2 does not appear to affect P granule formation, as the P granule markers PGL-1, CAR-1 and CGH-1 localized normally in nhl-2(ok818) mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and data not shown)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing normal localization of P granule markers in nhl-2(ok818) mutants

claim: CGH-1 is essential for fertility and localization of several P granule components
source: CGH-1 is essential for fertility and localization of several P granule components (Arnold et al., 2014; Sengupta and Boag, 2012; Boag et al., 2008; Audhya et al., 2005; Boag et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies

claim: In a cgh-1 loss of function mutant, NHL-2 localized normally
source: however in a cgh-1 loss of function mutant NHL-2 localized normally, while CAR-1 localized to 'sheet-like' structures in the gonad core (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C

claim: NHL-2 may contribute to germline gene regulation through different mechanisms than CGH-1
source: These data suggest that although NHL-2 has similar germline localization pattern to CGH-1 and functions with CGH-1 in the soma, NHL-2 may contribute to germline gene regulation through different mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that NHL-2 localization is independent of CGH-1

claim: A genome-wide RNAi screen identified 42 genes that when knocked down in the nhl-2(ok818) null background resulted in strong synthetic phenotypes
source: Out of 11,511 genes screened, we identified 42 genes, that when knocked down in the nhl-2(ok818) null background resulted in strong synthetic phenotypes, including sterility, embryonic lethality and larval arrest.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from a genome-wide RNAi screen

claim: Among the genetic interactors of nhl-2 are genes encoding factors required for biogenesis of the 22G-RNAs
source: Among the candidates are genes encoding factors required for biogenesis of the 22G-RNAs. These include the poly(U) polymerase CDE-1, along with the RdRP complex proteins EKL-1 (a dual Tudor domain protein) and DRH-3 (a Dicer related helicase), which have been shown to physically interact (Gu et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the RNAi screen and a citation to published work (Gu et al., 2009)

claim: CDE-1 was specifically implicated in the CSR-1 22G-RNA pathway
source: CDE-1 was specifically implicated in the CSR-1 22G-RNA pathway
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from the literature

claim: DRH-3 and EKL-1 function in both CSR-1 and WAGO 22G-RNA pathways
source: while DRH-3 and EKL-1 function in both CSR-1 and WAGO 22G-RNA pathways
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from the literature

claim: CSR-1 pathway components display defects in diakinetic chromosome organization similar to nhl-2(ok818) mutants
source: Notably, previous data demonstrated that CSR-1 pathway components display defects in diakinetic chromosome organization similar to nhl-2(ok818) mutants (Claycomb et al., 2009; She et al., 2009; van Wolfswinkel et al., 2009; Nakamura et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies

claim: Knockdown of drh-3, csr-1, ekl-1 or cde-1 in wild-type animals results in chromosome anomalies
source: Consistent with previous results, we observed chromosome anomalies when drh-3, csr-1, ekl-1 or cde-1 were knocked down in wild-type animals (Figure 2A–E)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-E and is consistent with previous results

claim: Knockdown of each 22G-RNA factor in nhl-2(ok818) mutants resulted in enhanced chromosomal aggregation at both 20°C and 25°C
source: Importantly, knockdown of each 22G-RNA factor in nhl-2(ok818) mutants resulted in enhanced chromosomal aggregation (Figure 2A–E) at both 20°C and 25°C
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-E

claim: nhl-2(ok818) double mutants with csr-1(tm892) or drh-3(ne4253) show enhanced diakinesis defects
source: We observed similar enhanced diakinesis defects in nhl-2(ok818) double mutants with csr-1(tm892) or drh-3(ne4253) (data not shown)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (though not shown in the manuscript)

claim: There is an increase in the embryonic lethality of nhl-2(ok818) animals depleted of CSR-1 pathway factors
source: Furthermore, and consistent with these chromosomal abnormalities, we observed an increase in the embryonic lethality of nhl-2(ok818) animals depleted of CSR-1 pathway factors, pointing to a strong genetic interaction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Loss of the CSR-1 pathway leads to aberrant accumulation of H3K9me2 on autosomes
source: Loss of the CSR-1 pathway leads to aberrant accumulation of H3K9me2 on autosomes and results in homologous pairing defects.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from the literature

claim: drh-3(ne4253) or csr-1(tm892) mutant males displayed abnormal accumulation of H3K9me2
source: Consistent with previous reports, drh-3(ne4253) or csr-1(tm892) mutant males displayed abnormal accumulation of H3K9me2 (She et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to published work (She et al., 2009)

claim: nhl-2(ok818) and nhl-2(ma372 ma399) males showed comparable patterns of abnormal H3K9me2 staining to drh-3 and csr-1 mutants
source: and interestingly, nhl-2(ok818) and nhl-2(ma372 ma399) males also showed comparable patterns of abnormal H3K9me2 staining (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: nhl-2(ok818) mutants have errors in MSUC and meiotic synapsis similar to drh-3(ne4253) or csr-1(tm892)
source: This abnormal enrichment of H3K9me2 on autosomes in nhl-2(ok818) germ cells suggests that nhl-2(ok818) mutants have errors in MSUC and meiotic synapsis similar to drh-3(ne4253) or csr-1(tm892)
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the H3K9me2 staining data

claim: Double mutants combinations of nhl-2(ok818) and csr-1(tm892) or drh-3(ne4253) exhibited no strong enhancement of the H3K9me2 phenotype
source: however, double mutants combinations of nhl-2(ok818) and csr-1(tm892) or drh-3(ne4253) exhibited no strong enhancement of this phenotype
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data

claim: Multiple components of small RNA pathways have been shown to be required for nuclear RNAi and germline immortality
source: Multiple components of small RNA pathways have been shown to be required for nuclear RNAi and germline immortality (Spracklin et al., 2017; Weiser et al., 2017; Ashe et al., 2012; Buckley et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies

claim: In wild-type animals, RNAi targeting lir-1 results in the silencing of the polycistronic pre-mRNA by the nuclear RNAi pathway, resulting in let-26 phenotypes of larval arrest and lethality
source: In wild-type animals, RNAi targeting lir-1 results in the silencing of the polycistronic pre-mRNA by the nuclear RNAi pathway, resulting in let-26 phenotypes of larval arrest and lethality (Figure 3A) (Bosher et al., 1999)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published work (Bosher et al., 1999) and illustrated in Figure 3A

claim: nhl-2(ok818) and nhl-2(ma372 ma399) animals were resistant to lir-1 RNAi
source: Interestingly, nhl-2(ok818) and nhl-2(ma372 ma399) animals were resistant to lir-1 RNAi and closely resembled nrde-2 and rde-4 nuclear RNAi mutants (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: The lir-1 RNAi resistance phenotype in nhl-2(ok818) was rescued by expressing a GFP-NHL-2 transgene in the soma
source: This resistance was rescued in nhl-2(ok818) worms expressing a GFP-NHL-2 transgene in the soma (Figure 3B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: After 10–12 generations, nhl-2(ok818) worms grown at 25°C became sterile
source: Consistent with the Mrt phenotype, after 10–12 generations nhl-2(ok818) worms grown at 25°C became sterile (Figure 3C) while wild-type worms remained fertile
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Similar Mrt results were obtained when nhl-2 was knocked down by continuous administration of RNAi at 25°C and with nhl-2(ma372 ma399)
source: Similar results were obtained when nhl-2 was knocked down by continuous administration of RNAi at 25°C and with nhl-2(ma372 ma399) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C

claim: When the F1 generation of nhl-2(ok818) worms were moved at the L1 stage from 25°C to 20°C, it took three generations for the brood size to recover to the normal nhl-2(ok818) level
source: As has been demonstrated for other Mrt mutants (Spracklin et al., 2017; Ni et al., 2016), when the F1 generation of nhl-2(ok818) worms were moved at the L1 stage to 20°C it took three generations for the brood size to recover to the normal nhl-2(ok818) level (Figure 3D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and citations to published studies

claim: Embryonic lethality in nhl-2(ok818) took a generation to recover to the nhl-2(ok818) 20°C level after temperature shift
source: and embryonic lethality took a generation to recover to the nhl-2(ok818) 20°C level (Figure 3E)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Similar transgenerational recovery results were obtained using nhl-2(ma372 ma399) mutants
source: Similar results were obtained using nhl-2(ma372 ma399) mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E

claim: NHL-2 was partially required for RNAi inheritance, as 14% of the worms were GFP positive in the F1 generation, compared to 0% for N2 worms and 84% and 88% for nrde-2(mj168) and hrde-1(tm1200) worms, respectively
source: We found that NHL-2 was partially required for RNAi inheritance, as 14% of the worms were GFP positive in the F1 generation, compared to 0% for N2 worms and 84% and 88% for nrde-2(mj168) and hrde-1(tm1200) worms, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RNAi inheritance assays

claim: Similar RNAi inheritance results were obtained using nhl-2(ma372 ma399) mutants
source: Similar results were obtained using nhl-2(ma372 ma399) mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F

claim: NHL-2 participates in nuclear RNAi and multigenerational epigenetic inheritance pathways
source: Together these data are consistent with NHL-2 participating in nuclear RNAi and multigenerational epigenetic inheritance pathways.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the lir-1 RNAi resistance, Mrt phenotype, and RNAi inheritance data

claim: DRH-3 and NHL-2 physically interact by co-IP
source: First, DRH-3 and NHL-2 physically interact by co-IP.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation experiments

claim: CSR-1 associates with NHL-2 by co-IP in adult hermaphrodites
source: Indeed, we found that CSR-1 associates with NHL-2 by co-IP in adult hermaphrodites (Figure 4A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: NHL-2 interacts with the RdRP complex helicase, DRH-3
source: We then moved on to test for interactions with other members of the CSR-1 pathway by similar experiments, and found an interaction between NHL-2 and the RdRP complex helicase, DRH-3 (Gu et al., 2009) (Figure 4B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and a citation to published work (Gu et al., 2009)

claim: GST-NHL-2 associated with both CSR-1 and HRDE-1 from whole adult worm lysates, but not WAGO-1, or other components of the EGO-1, RRF-1 or EKL-1
source: In these experiments, we observed that GST-NHL-2 associated with both CSR-1 and HRDE-1 from whole adult worm lysates, but not WAGO-1, or other components of the EGO-1, RRF-1 or EKL-1 (Figure 4C, data not shown)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: NHL-2 associates with CSR-1 and HRDE-1 pathway proteins at multiple points of pathway activity
source: These data indicate that NHL-2 associates with CSR-1 and HRDE-1 pathway proteins at multiple points of pathway activity (with DRH-3 of the RdRP complex and with AGO effectors of the RISC)
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the co-IP and GST pulldown data

claim: CSR-1 protein levels are comparable in wild-type and nhl-2(ok818) animals
source: We observed comparable levels of both CSR-1 and DRH-3 protein in wild-type and nhl-2(ok818) animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and data not shown for DRH-3)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: The association of NHL-2 and CSR-1 is not related to potential E3 ubiquitin ligase activity by NHL-2
source: suggesting that the association of NHL-2 and CSR-1 is not related to potential E3 ubiquitin ligase activity by NHL-2
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that CSR-1 levels are not affected in nhl-2 mutants

claim: The overall size and first nucleotide distributions of small RNA species in nhl-2(ok818) mutants are consistent with the wild-type controls at both temperatures
source: The overall size and first nucleotide distributions of small RNA species in nhl-2(ok818) mutants are consistent with the wild-type controls at both temperatures (Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2

claim: There was an overall decrease in 21U-RNAs at 25°C compared with 20°C, for both wild-type and nhl-2(ok818) mutants
source: There was an overall decrease in 21U-RNAs at 25°C compared with 20°C, for both wild-type and nhl-2(ok818) mutants (Figure 5—figure supplements 1, 2 and 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1, 2 and 3

claim: 21-23nt siRNA levels increased slightly in both wild-type and nhl-2(ok818) mutants at 25°C compared to 20°C
source: 21-23nt siRNA levels (which encompass the 22G-RNA category) increased slightly in both wild-type and nhl-2(ok818) mutants at 25°C compared to 20°C
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data

claim: miRNA levels were relatively unchanged in both strains between temperatures
source: while miRNA levels were relatively unchanged in both strains between temperatures (Figure 5—figure supplements 1, 2 and 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1, 2 and 3

claim: There was a consistent decrease in 22G-RNA and 26G-RNA populations in nhl-2(ok818) mutants relative to wild-type at 25°C
source: We observed a consistent decrease in 22G-RNA and 26G-RNA populations in nhl-2(ok818) mutants relative to wild-type at 25°C (Figure 5—figure supplements 1, 2 and 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1, 2 and 3

claim: Concomitant with the 22G-RNA decreases, there was an increase in the proportion of miRNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants
source: Concomitant with the 22G-RNA decreases, we observed an increase in the proportion of miRNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data

claim: The increase in miRNA proportion in nhl-2(ok818) mutants is likely due to a 'filling in' of the cloning space when small RNA populations are expressed as a proportion of the total reads
source: While it is possible that this change in miRNAs is biologically meaningful, it is more likely due to a 'filling in' of the cloning space when small RNA populations are expressed as a proportion of the total reads, as previous reports observed little change in miRNA levels in nhl-2(ok818) mutants (Hammell et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data and a citation to published work (Hammell et al., 2009)

claim: There were decreases in the 21U-RNA populations of nhl-2(ok818) mutants relative to wild-type at 20°C, which are not evident at 25°C
source: Finally, we observed decreases in the 21U-RNA populations of nhl-2(ok818) mutants relative to wild-type at 20°C, which are not evident at 25°C
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data

claim: 573 and 724 genes display a two-fold or greater depletion of 22G-RNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants relative to wild-type at 20°C and 25°C respectively, with 381 genes in common between the two temperatures
source: We observed that 573 and 724 genes display a two-fold or greater depletion of 22G-RNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants relative to wild-type at 20°C and 25°C respectively, with 381 genes in common between the two temperatures (the top-right Venn-pie diagram in Figure 5A)
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The genes depleted of 22G-RNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants at 20°C are enriched in WAGO-1 and HRDE-1 target genes
source: The genes depleted of 22G-RNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants at 20°C are enriched in WAGO-1 and HRDE-1 target genes (Figure 5A), comprising 36.5% (209/573; hypergeometric test q-value or q = 9.6E-80) and 36.6% (210/573; q = 2.1E-83), respectively, with 66 genes shared between the two WAGOs
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: 74.5% (427/573) of genes depleted of 22G-RNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants at 20°C were depleted of 22G-RNAs in a 12-fold wago mutant
source: Consistent with this result, 74.5% (427/573; q = 1.6E-296) of these genes were depleted of 22G-RNAs in a mutant strain that carries mutations in twelve wago (12-fold wago mutant including mutations in hrde-1 and wago-1 [Gu et al., 2009])
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data and statistical analysis

claim: 33% (189/573) of genes depleted of 22G-RNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants at 20°C are CSR-1 targets
source: Notably, 33% (189/573; q = 3.7E-5) of these genes are CSR-1 targets, with only 17 of these genes overlapping with HRDE-1 or WAGO-1 targets
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data and statistical analysis

claim: 29.3% of the 724 genes depleted of 22G-RNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants at 25°C are CSR-1 target genes
source: Similar to the results at 20°C, 29.3% of the 724 genes depleted of 22G-RNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants at 25°C are CSR-1 target genes (212/724; q = 3.7E-2)
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data and statistical analysis

claim: 33.7% and 37.2% of genes depleted of 22G-RNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants at 25°C are WAGO-1 and HRDE-1 targets
source: while 33.7% and 37.2% are WAGO-1 and HRDE-1 targets (244/724 and 269/724; q = 2.1E-85 and 4.7E-110; with 139 genes in common)
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data and statistical analysis

claim: Nearly 78% (563/724) of the genes depleted of 22G-RNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants at 25°C overlap with genes depleted of small RNAs in the 12-fold wago mutant
source: Nearly 78% (563/724, q < 1E-300) of the genes depleted of 22G-RNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants at 25°C overlap with genes depleted of small RNAs in the 12-fold wago mutant
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data and statistical analysis

claim: The majority of genes depleted of 22G-RNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants at either temperature significantly overlap with genes depleted of 22G-RNAs in RdRP complex mutants, ekl-1(tm1599), ego-1(om97), and drh-3(ne4253)
source: Finally, the majority of genes depleted of 22G-RNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants at either temperature significantly overlap with genes depleted of 22G-RNAs in RdRP complex mutants, ekl-1(tm1599), ego-1(om97), and drh-3(ne4253) (all q-values < 7.3E-195) (Figure 5A)
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: 83.8% (480/573) and 83.4% (604/724) of the genes depleted of 22G-RNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants at 20°C and 25°C, respectively, are also depleted of 22G-RNAs in glp-4(bn2) mutants
source: Consistent with the role of NHL-2 in fertility and germ cell development (Figures 1 and 2), 83.8% (480/573, q = 2.6E-166) and 83.4% (604/724 q = 3.9E-209) of the genes depleted of 22G-RNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants at 20°C and 25°C, respectively, are also depleted of 22G-RNAs in glp-4(bn2) mutants (Figure 5A)
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: The genes depleted of 22G-RNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants are targeted by 22G-RNAs in the germline
source: These data indicate that the genes depleted of 22G-RNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants are targeted by 22G-RNAs in the germline.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the overlap with glp-4(bn2) data

claim: 58.4% (423/724) and 61.6% (353/573) of the genes depleted of 22G-RNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants at 25°C and 20°C respectively overlap with genes generally expressed in the gonad
source: Further comparison with the male- and female-specific gonad gene expression data indicated that 58.4% (423/724; q-value = 0.0128) and 61.6% (353/573; q-value = 1E-4) of the genes depleted of 22G-RNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants at 25°C and 20°C respectively overlap with genes generally expressed in the gonad (meaning that they are expressed in both the spermatogenic or oogenic gonads) (Figure 5B)
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: There is a statistically significant enrichment for oogenic genes in the nhl-2(ok818) depleted gene sets
source: We observed a subtle, but statistically significant enrichment for oogenic genes in the nhl-2(ok818) depleted gene sets (16.4%, 119/724 genes at 25°C, q = 2.2E-11, 22.5%, 129/573 genes at 20°C, q-value = 2.7E-24)
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data and statistical analysis

claim: In wild-type worms, 22G-RNAs are distributed across the entire length of WAGO target genes and are present in greater abundance than CSR-1 22G-RNAs
source: In wild-type worms, 22G-RNAs are distributed across the entire length of WAGO target genes and are present in greater abundance than CSR-1 22G-RNAs.
evidence: The claim is supported by metagene analysis of small RNA sequencing data

claim: CSR-1 target genes generally have fewer 22G-RNAs targeting them overall, with a slight bias in small RNA coverage toward the 5´ end
source: Conversely, CSR-1 target genes generally have fewer 22G-RNAs targeting them overall, with a slight bias in small RNA coverage toward the 5´ end.
evidence: The claim is supported by metagene analysis of small RNA sequencing data

claim: For WAGO target genes in nhl-2(ok818) mutants relative to wild-type, the distribution of 22G-RNAs was only mildly changed over the metagene length at either temperature
source: For the set of WAGO target genes in nhl-2(ok818) mutants relative to wild-type, we noted that the distribution of 22G-RNAs was only mildly changed over the metagene length at either temperature (Figure 5D,E, Figure 5—figure supplements 5 and 6)
evidence: The claim is supported by metagene analysis shown in Figure 5D,E and Figure 5—figure supplements 5 and 6

claim: There is a subtle yet statistically significant decrease in the small RNAs toward the 3´ end of WAGO target genes at both 20°C and 25°C in nhl-2(ok818) mutants
source: We noted, however, a subtle yet statistically significant decrease in the small RNAs toward the 3´ end of WAGO target genes at both 20°C and 25°C, in which the centroid of the 22G-RNA distribution for WAGO-1 targets shifts by 0.5% of the metagene length towards the 5´ end and the distribution for HRDE-1 targets shifts by 1.2% of the metagene length toward the 5´ end at 20°C (Wilcoxon rank-sum test p-value=8.55E-03, p-value=6.09E-03, respectively; Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplements 5 and 6)
evidence: The claim is supported by metagene analysis and statistical testing shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplements 5 and 6

claim: For CSR-1 target genes, the distribution of 22G-RNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants was distinct from that in wild-type worms
source: For CSR-1 target genes, the distribution of 22G-RNAs in nhl-2(ok818) mutants was distinct from that in wild-type worms, and striking in comparison to WAGO target genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by metagene analysis of small RNA sequencing data

claim: At both 20°C and 25°C, there was a significant decrease in the abundance of 22G-RNAs over the 5´ half of CSR-1 target genes in nhl-2(ok818) mutants relative to wild-type controls
